47	\section{The Static Arguments of a Call}
48	\seclabel{static-arg-inference}
49	
50	The static arguments of a call that does not write them are found in two
51	steps: the declaration that the call invokes is chosen first, and it is
52	instantiated second.
53	
54	\emph{Choice.}
55	The declaration is chosen as \secref{resolving-coercion} describes.
56	A declaration with static parameters is applicable to a call, without or with
57	coercion, if some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their bounds is
58	applicable to the call.
59	Declarations are compared on the parameter types they declare, a declaration
60	with static parameters on its parameter types taken over every instance that
61	its bounds allow, and not on an instance inferred for the call.
62	So a coercion is applied only to make a call possible: it never changes which
63	declaration is chosen when one is applicable to the call without it.
64	
65	\emph{Instantiation.}
66	The static arguments of the chosen declaration are then inferred, and with them
67	the instance of the declaration that the call invokes:
68	\begin{itemize}
69	\item A type parameter, or a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter, that the
70	declared type of a parameter mentions other than as the whole type, as
71	\EXP{b\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} mentions \VAR{T}, is fixed by
72	the argument at that position, whose type must be a subtype of the parameter
73	type of the instance.
74	\item Where the call has an expected type (below), a type parameter that the
75	declared return type mentions other than as the whole type is fixed by the
76	expected type as well.
77	\item A type parameter that is the whole declared type of one or more
78	parameters, as \VAR{T} is of \EXP{x\COLON{}T}, and that is not fixed as above,
79	takes, among the types of the arguments at those positions and the types to
80	which they can be coerced, the narrowest under $\morespecificeq$
81	(\secref{resolving-coercion}) that every one of those arguments is
82	substitutable for (\secref{applicability-with-coercion}) and that the bounds of
83	the type parameter permit.
84	For number arguments this is the narrowest type into which every one of them
85	converts: \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and a
86	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and also for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and an
87	\EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though neither of them is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
88	(\secref{basic-integers}).
89	Where there is no such narrowest type, and the rule for numerals
90	(\secref{numeral-default}) does not settle the tie, the type parameter takes
91	the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has
92	none (\secref{type-param}), and what the expected type (below), where the call
93	has one, requires of the declared return type, provided the types of those
94	arguments are subtypes of it; none of those arguments is converted.
95	\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 gave such
96	a type parameter the union of the types of those arguments; on 29~September 2026
97	the revival took the rule by which the dispatcher of the type group's paper of
98	2019 instantiates a type parameter, which gives the bound.}
99	\item A type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes as
100	above, such as a type parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole
101	type, likewise takes the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound,
102	\TYP{Any} if it has none (\secref{type-param}), and what the expected type
103	(below), where the call has one, requires of the declared return type.
104	Inference never instantiates a static parameter at \TYP{BottomType}, which
105	programmers must not write (\secref{bottom-type}).
106	So, for the declaration
107	\EXP{\VAR{stop}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(s\COLON\TYP{String})\COLON{}T}, the
108	variable declaration
109	\EXP{x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = \VAR{stop}(\hbox{\rm``\STR{no}''})} instantiates
110	\VAR{stop} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the same call with no expected type
111	instantiates it at \TYP{Any}.
112	\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 did not
113	describe such a type parameter and left open whether inference may give it
114	\TYP{BottomType}, which the team's draft note at the end of this chapter asks.
115	The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that the rule by which the dispatcher of
116	the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a type parameter that the arguments
117	do not fix, the intersection of its upper bounds, which never instantiates a
118	type parameter at \TYP{BottomType}, is the rule of static inference as well.}
119	\item Every argument is then admitted against the corresponding parameter type
120	of the instance by substitutability: an argument whose type is a subtype of it
121	is passed as it is, and any other argument is coerced to it
122	(\secref{coercion}), as an argument is coerced to the declared type of a
123	parameter of a declaration without static parameters.
124	\end{itemize}
125	The coercions that the instance needs are inserted into the call statically,
126	as is any coercion that \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses.
127	
128	\emph{The expected type.}
129	A call has an expected type in these contexts: as the right-hand side of a
130	variable or field declaration that declares its type, that type; as the
131	right-hand side of an assignment to a variable whose type is declared, that
132	type; as the body of a functional that declares its return type, that type;
133	as the last expression of a block that has an expected type, whether or not
134	local declarations precede it in the block, the block's expected type; as a
135	branch of an \KWD{if} expression with an \KWD{else} clause that has an
136	expected type, the expected type of the \KWD{if} expression; as a clause of an
137	\KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, \TYP{()}, the type that
138	every such clause must have (\secref{if-expr}); as a clause of a
139	\KWD{typecase} expression that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause
140	among them, the expected type of the \KWD{typecase} expression, of which the
141	union of the types of its clauses, the type of the \KWD{typecase} expression
142	(\secref{typecase}), is then a subtype where the type of each clause is; and
143	as the body of a \KWD{label} expression that has an expected type, or as the
144	\KWD{with} clause expression of an \KWD{exit} expression whose target is that
145	\KWD{label} expression, the expected type of the \KWD{label} expression, of
146	which the union of the type of its body and the types of those \KWD{with}
147	clause values, the type of the \KWD{label} expression (\secref{label-expr}),
148	is then a subtype where each of those types is.
149	The expected type is used whether the call is written by tight juxtaposition,
150	as \EXP{f(x)} (\secref{juxtameaning}), or by loose juxtaposition, as
151	\EXP{f\;x}, or as a method invocation or an operator application.
152	\revision{revival-expected-contexts}{The revival's text of 29~September 2026
153	gave the last expression of a block an expected type only where no local
154	declaration precedes it, and gave none to a clause of an \KWD{if} expression
155	without an \KWD{else} clause, to a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression or to
156	a call written by loose juxtaposition; the revival decided on 8~October 2026
157	that each has the type that the text already requires of it.
158	Its text of 8~October 2026 gave none to the body of a \KWD{label} expression
159	or to the \KWD{with} clause expression of an \KWD{exit} expression; the
160	revival decided on 9~October 2026 that they have the expected type of the
161	\KWD{label} expression, as a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression has that of
162	the \KWD{typecase} expression.}
163	The return type of the instance that the steps above find must be a subtype of
164	the expected type.
165	If they find no such instance, the static arguments are inferred again without
166	the expected type, and the call is accepted only if the return type of the instance
167	then found is a subtype of the expected type or can be coerced to it; in the
168	second case the result of the call is coerced to the expected type
169	(\secref{coercion}).
170	So, for the declarations
171	\EXP{\VAR{wrap}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
172	and \EXP{\VAR{id}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T},
173	the variable declaration \EXP{a\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket = \VAR{wrap}(3)}
174	instantiates \VAR{wrap} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, which the expected type fixes,
175	and coerces the numeral, while \EXP{b\COLON\mathbb{Z}64 = \VAR{id}(3)}
176	instantiates \VAR{id} at the numeral's own type (\secref{literals}) and coerces
177	the result.
178	
179	\emph{Dispatch.}
180	The call, with the coercions of its instance inserted, dispatches at run time
181	as \secref{resolving-overloading} describes, by subtyping and without further
182	coercion, to the most specific declaration applicable to the converted values.
183	
184	For example, of the declarations
185	\EXP{\VAR{op}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Number}\rrbracket(a\COLON{}T, b\COLON{}T)}
186	and \EXP{\VAR{op}(a\COLON\TYP{Any}, b\COLON\TYP{Any})}, the call
187	\EXP{\VAR{op}(z, w)}, where \VAR{z} has type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \VAR{w} has
188	type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, chooses the first, which is applicable without
189	coercion, since its instance at \TYP{Number} is, and is more specific than the
190	second; the first is instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \VAR{z} is coerced,
191	and the converted call runs that instance.
192	\revision{revival-inference}{The interpreter has no static types and applies
193	the same rule at dispatch, from the run-time types of the arguments: it infers
194	the static arguments of a declaration with static parameters with coercion,
195	and instantiates the declaration that its dispatch chooses by the rule for a
196	type parameter that is a parameter's whole type.
197	So where the declared type of a variable is wider than the type of its value,
198	or an argument's static type is \TYP{Any}, it may run a declaration at a
199	narrower instance than the compiled path, which instantiates it at the static
200	types.
201	Where neither an argument's type nor a type into which the arguments convert is
202	the narrowest, it gives a type parameter that is the whole type of parameters
203	its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, as this chapter does: for a
204	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, \TYP{Number} where that is the

206	\KWD{extends} clause.
207	It does the same where the arguments that fix a type parameter inside other

211	itself or another, or that is declared with several bounds that the interpreter

213	other: such a type parameter it binds, as before, to the narrowest named common
214	supertype of the arguments' run-time types that the bounds permit, where there
215	is one, and where there is none a call that fixes a type parameter of the
216	second kind fails (row~591 of the revival's gap ledger).
217	When its dispatch chooses among declarations, it passes over a declaration with
218	static parameters whose arguments have several minimal common supertypes in
219	favour of any other declaration applicable to the call without coercion
220	(row~589 of the revival's gap ledger).
221	It does not yet fix a type parameter by the expected type.
222	A type parameter that an argument bounds only from above, as a function
223	argument bounds the type parameter of its parameter type, it instantiates at the
224	intersection of the upper bounds that its declared bound and the arguments
225	place on it: at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} for a function of a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} where

228	\TYP{Number}; such a type parameter whose bound mentions a
229	static parameter, or that is declared with several bounds that it cannot meet,

5	\subsection{The contexts that give a call an expected type}
6	\seclabel{revival-expected-contexts}
7	
8	\begin{description}
9	\item[Affected sections] \secref{static-arg-inference}; \secref{numeral-default}.
10	\item[Change] The list of the contexts in which a call has an expected type,
11	in \secref{static-arg-inference}, gives the last expression of a block the
12	block's expected type whether or not local declarations precede it, and gains
13	two contexts: a clause of an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause,
14	whose expected type is \TYP{()}, and a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression
15	that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause among them, whose expected
16	type is that of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
17	The sentence after the list says that the expected type is used also for a call
18	written by loose juxtaposition, as \EXP{f\;x}.
19	A second revision adds a third context to the list: the body of a \KWD{label}
20	expression that has an expected type, and the \KWD{with} clause expression of
21	each \KWD{exit} expression whose target is that \KWD{label} expression, whose
22	expected type is that of the \KWD{label} expression.
23	The item of the list of what the chapter does not yet describe, in
24	\secref{numeral-default}, names an argument of another call and the body of a
25	\KWD{for} loop, and no longer names the contexts that the list of contexts now
26	gives, the body of a \KWD{label} expression among them.
27	Each changed passage has a box.
28	How a call is instantiated under its expected type is unchanged.
29	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
30	revival's decision of 8~October 2026 that these four contexts give a call the
31	type that the text already requires of them, a clause of a \KWD{typecase}
32	expression by the rule for the type of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
33	The text gives each context its type.
34	``If there is no \KWD{else} clause in an \KWD{if} expression, then every clause
35	must have type \EXP{()}'' (\secref{if-expr}).
36	``If the last element of the expression block is an expression, the value and
37	type of this expression are the value and type of the expression block as a
38	whole'' (\secref{block-expr}), whatever local declarations precede it.
39	The static arguments of an identifier reference ``are statically inferred from
40	the context of the function call'' (\secref{idn-ref}), however the call is
41	written.
42	``The type of a \KWD{typecase} expression is the union of types of all
43	right-hand sides of the typecase clauses'' (\secref{typecase}), which is a
44	subtype of the expected type when the type of each clause is.
45	Since the revival's decision of 29~September 2026 a type parameter that nothing
46	at a call fixes takes the intersection of its upper bounds, never
47	\TYP{BottomType} (\secref{revival-inference}), so a call of \VAR{fail} or
48	\VAR{builtinPrimitive} of \library, whose type parameter only the result
49	mentions, took the bound \TYP{Any} in these contexts, and the compiled type
50	checker refused thirteen such calls of \library\ that the interpreter runs
51	(row~560 of the revival's gap ledger).
52	The alternative not taken was that the library write the static argument at
53	each such call, as \EXP{\VAR{fail}\llbracket()\rrbracket(s)}: the revival
54	decided that the library's own practice is the standard, and the library does
55	not route round a gap of the type checker.
56	A reversal would take the four contexts out of the list of contexts and back
57	into the item, and the compiled type checker would refuse those calls again.
58	The second revision follows the revival's decision of 9~October 2026 that the
59	body of a \KWD{label} expression and the \KWD{with} clause values of its exits
60	take the expected type of the whole \KWD{label} expression, as the clauses of a
61	\KWD{typecase} expression take that of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
62	``The type of a \KWD{label} expression is the union of the type of the last
63	expression of its expression block and the types of the \KWD{with} clause
64	values of any \KWD{exit} expressions within the \KWD{label} expression whose
65	target is the \KWD{label} expression's name'' (\secref{label-expr}), which is a
66	subtype of the expected type when each of those types is.
67	The thirteenth of the calls of \library\ above ends a clause of a
68	\KWD{typecase} expression that ends the body of a \KWD{label} expression, and
69	took the bound \TYP{Any} there (row~642 of the revival's gap ledger).
70	A reversal of the second revision would take the body of a \KWD{label}
71	expression and its exits' \KWD{with} clause values out of the list of contexts
72	and back into the item, and the compiled type checker would refuse that call
73	again.
74	The full reasoning is in
75	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-expected-type/REPORT.md}
76	and, for the second revision, in
77	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-contexts/REPORT.md}
78	in the revival's repository.
79	\item[Effect] The compiled type checker gives these contexts their expected
80	types: it checks a clause of an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else}
81	clause against \TYP{()}, and it gives the expected type of the enclosing
82	expression to the last expression of a block after local declarations, to a
83	clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression, to the body of a \KWD{label} expression
84	and the \KWD{with} clause expressions of its exits, and to the application that
85	a loose juxtaposition makes.
